$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 4\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,C={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the bases $B$ and $C$ of ${R}^{2},$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $B$, shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$

activity_context.topic_title: Connections Between Matrix Representations of a Linear Transformation

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Matrix of a Linear Transformation Relative to a Given Basis
examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/76bfd9209f632ac8576051154d7e4250d8c4c53ffe843238b6d25835704ce398.png)

Consider the bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2,$ and the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ with respect to the basis $\mathcal{B}$, shown above. Find the matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$
examples.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}}^{-1},
$$

where $P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/cb0c35da5a4bd26c92343d7262efcb7ba7f197cdeea95c2d541b7441a6485804.png)

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/6759e7c098d5375894d540050e3c3dd9e3bb453b0cac7338b9b6754bb635f717.png)

Now, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{C}}} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-0\cdot (-1)}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C} \mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -3 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -9 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -7 \\ 2 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem:
$$
B={[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]},\,[T]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the basis $B$ of ${R}^{2}$ and the matrix $[T]_{B}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to this basis. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the basis $B$ and standard basis $S$ is given by the following diagram:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14067267/assets/dbd020362f950fe8bfb4c592652b9e78a73610fa01a247b0b7ead6f201bf9ea5.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},
$$

and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $S$ is

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to S}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot (-3)-(-1)\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the standard basis $S:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{S} & ={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
